There's a Kudu on My Stoep

By: Kate Barry | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Marloth Park - the bush veld holiday town shared by thousands of humans and wild animals. But there's nothing left to eat, and culling is illegal.

Unique Selling Point:
It's unique in the country: an enclosed suburb, a sunset to sunrise curfew, wild animals dependent on humans for feeding, and the local municipality the only managing authority.
It seemed like a good idea at the time. In 1977 Marloth Park was established as a holiday town bordering the Kruger National Park. The animals could come and go as they pleased by simply crossing the Crocodile river. But years later, when foot & mouth disease and TB became a concern, veterinary services installed a fence, effectively capturing the game inside Marloth Park.
Now, 47 years and 3800 home owners later, it's over-crowded, over-grazed and the animals are dying of starvation.

Summary:
Marloth Park holds 4500 residential stands each measuring 1500 m2. In between the stands are parklands which are meant for grazing. But overpopulation and mismanagement of the wildlife means there is hardly anything for the animals to eat.
In 2001 the Nkomazi Local Municipality took over Marloth Park. Since then there has been no Environmental Management Plan adopted or implemented by the NKLM. Unlike other wildlife estates, there is no special levy. Residents only pay normal and fairly low municipal rates.
In 2015, NKLM (who employ a Conservation manager and 12 game rangers) began a culling programme, taking off hundreds of animals to relieve the situation. But the carcasses were taken to the Mauricedale Abattoir for processing, which is across the N4, the red line which denotes a foot & mouth area. The meat was then sold with the proceeds going to the Municipality. But meat cannot be traded across the red line. In 2016 the culling programme continued, with rangers hunting animals at night, between the houses, using spotlights. However, there were reports of bullets flying through windows and into walls, thereby endangering the residents.
In 2017 the Marloth Park Ratepayers Association brought an urgent interdict to stop the culling between the houses as it is illegal to shoot in a residential area without good cause, it was dangerous and put lives and properties at risk. Since then there has been a population explosion, both in animals and humans, and the Municipality seems unable to enforce basic by-laws, never mind an EMP.
Neighbouring reserves like Mjejane and Sabie Sands has offered to take impala etc off their hands but the Municipality regards the animals as their assets and they want to cash in on the meat. Currently the rangers are allowed to shoot sick or injured animals, and are also picking up animals that have died from starvation. The count is between 60 and 70 animals per month.
Within Marloth Park is another game reserve called Lionspruit. A solution put forward has been to capture game in temporary bomas and transport them to Lionspruit for culling.




Further information:
Within Marloth Park is another game reserve called Lionspruit. A solution put forward has been to capture game in temporary bomas and transport them to Lionspruit for culling. NKLM put out a tender for this, but has not received a suitable bid.
They are also building an abattoir attached to the Rangers' living quarters where they plan to process carcasses. But they already seem to be using this facility as CB found a warthog head perched on bags of meat in the cold room.
Adding to the complication is an ongoing catfight between the various organisations within Marloth Park. The Ratepayers Association (560), the Property Owners Association (150), the Honorary Rangers, Marlothii Conservancy cannot agree on how the stalemate should be resolved and by whom.
1. NKLM is incompetent and not following best practice - animals are overbred, Marloth Park is over-utilised. Such mismanagement that it is becoming an ethical issue.
2. The Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Authority should have stepped in as nature conservation is a provincial competency.
3. Conflict between the residents has led to a failure of ethical wildlife management.

Extra Budget Items:
3 day-shoot
1 travel day
Car hire - large enough for 4 crew + baggage + gear
Fuel for roughly 1000km
Toll fees
Accommodation for 4 people
S&T for 4 people

Script:


A KUDU ON MY STOEP


V/O: It seemed like a good idea at the time: your own home in the bushveld, a piece of paradise where animals wander freely. No fences, no predators, just you and your neighbours and the game under the African sky. What could possibly go wrong?


Chris: The wildlife management here, it’s obviously been shocking in past.

Dawie: If there was a proper management plan, you would never get to the point where the population escalates to what it has.

Cindy: We are now so developed. It’s just house on house on house on house.

Brian: The herbaceous layer for grazing animals has been largely destroyed.

V/O: A lone blue wildebeest is looking for something to eat.

Chris: Our animals are very, very hungry. They’re starving.

V/O The property owner calls the rangers to take a look.

Chris: But now it’s coming to a head. Something is going to have to be done soon, soon, soon.

V/O: The ranger lifts his rifle and takes aim.

FADE TO BLACK

V/O: Established in 1977 Marloth Park is a holiday town in a far corner of Mpumalanga. The Crocodile River flows in a horseshoe shape around its borders. In the middle is the Lionspruit Nature Reserve. To the north is the Kruger National Park, and to the south is the N4 highway.

It’s become a popular place for tourists, with a range of accommodation –from upmarket game lodges to a basic rondawel. But with over 4500 residential stands and 3800 homeowners, there is bound to be a clash. Some residents have been here for decades and enjoy the traditional bushveld ways. Others are newcomers, keen to cash in on the commercial opportunities.

Sfx: Hier kom die bokke! Hier kom die bokke!

V/O: The sunset to sunrise curfew may be ignored by some residents but come morning nearly two thousand workers report for duty. Run by the Nkomazi Local Municipality Marloth Park is essentially a fenced suburb with wild animals.

Link: One would ask why don’t they just drop the fences and let the animals go into the Kruger? But you can’t because there’s a huge risk of diseases like foot-and-mouth and TB.

V/O: Marloth Park is unique, but that’s the cause of significant problems. Too many animals, not enough food, nowhere to go – so who’s responsible?

Cindy: The municipality took over in 2001.You must remember conservation management is not a normal municipal function and they’re lacking. They’re totally incompetent when it comes to conservation management.

V/O: Cindy Benson is the chairperson of the Marloth Park Ratepayers Association and believes this incompetence has led to the current crisis.

Cindy: The last time there was a fire burn done was in 2008. So, if you have a look at an aerial photograph of Marloth Park compared to adjoining Kruger National Park, they’re a savannah, we’re a thicket. There is no bush clearing, there’s no burns. So, due to that fact, there’s no grass growing.

Evan: It was overpopulated already in 2015. And that’s why you have no grazing, you have no browsing.

V/O: Evan Powell represents another resident organisation, the Marloth Park Property Owners Association. They blame the lack of food on too many animals.

Evan: In 2015 and 16 there was game removal, and it was very effective. But even then, there was still an excess of game left in Marloth.

V/O: The Municipality employs a Conservation Manager and 12 rangers. They embarked on a culling programme in 2015 to reduce the number of hungry herbivores. But many residents were outraged.

Cindy: The property owners were up in arms. There was constant shooting between the houses.

Marlene: It was late afternoon, between four and five.

V/O: This woman wants to hide her identity for fear of being targeted.

Marlene: I was sitting in my swimming pool that's close to the road. And they came driving up and they shot that kudu cow right in front of me while I'm sitting in the pool. What if - I know now the way these guys shoot because they normally shoot an animal that's hurt or anything five, six shots before they kill it.

Dawie: I was sitting inside my house one evening watching television. I heard the shot, and it was right in front of my house, and I thought this is not on.

V/O: Dawie Fourie has lived in Marloth Park for 27 years and belongs to the Ratepayers’ Association.

Dawie: And we started enquiring like where is your licence to hunt. They couldn’t produce a licence. No competency certificate, and the gun didn’t belong to the person shooting. It belongs to the municipality. So, you actually had to have a letter from the municipality authorizing to use it. So, he had none of the documentation with him. All the houses from where he shot that animal was within less than 60 metres of where he was shooting.

V/O: But Evan believes these fears were exaggerated.

Mac: So, there was monitoring and supervision, they weren’t just going willy-nilly and shooting?

Evan: Not a chance. I mean, we would issue them bullets. And at the end of the session, you count the carcasses, you count the bullets. You know, it's not just a haring around here and blasting away. Not at all.

Cindy: It’s not good practice because of the risk factor. And they were using an abattoir that was 37km away from Marloth Park over the red line, what we call the red line because this is a foot and mouth area.

V/O: The N4 is the Red Line, a veterinary fence that controls the spread of animal diseases. The Ratepayers felt so strongly that they took the Municipality to Court. In 2017 they obtained an interdict against the shooting of animals in Marloth Park.

Prof: Technically the interdict put a stop to the culling of animals, but the issue was not culling animals. The issue was using high powered rifles in a residential area.

V/O: Professor Brian Reilly teaches at the University of the Free State and is former Head of Department of Nature Conservation at Tshwane University of Technology. In 2018 he did a veld assessment of Marloth Park.

Prof: The number of animals, the biomass of animals have exceeded the resource’s ability to carry them. So now, in that situation, the only option you have is to either remove the animals or to supplementary feed the animals.

V/O: And with culling at an end, that’s what’s been happening in Marloth Park for years. This huge delivery of grass was donated by one of the homeowners. Residents collect their bales along with buckets of molasses to mix with the grass.

Spar link: So, to show you how dire and serious the situation is. This is a shopping centre in Marloth Park, but it’s the only Spar in the country that sells game feed. Let’s go check.

V/O: It was sold out, but the manager gave us their monthly sales volume.
.
Deleen: I’ve worked it out at about 1080 5kg bags a month.

Mac: That’s a lot hey?

Deleen: It’s a lot.

V/O: In fact, that works out to 5.6 tons of pellets sold at that outlet alone.
Then there’s a small business that delivers 40kg bags to residents. They move 3.2 tons of game pellets per week. They also deliver 20kg bales of lucerne – 300 of them per week. They’re supplying almost 37 tons of game feed per month.

Chris: Ja, without the homeowners in Marloth, there wouldn’t be a live animal on Marloth right now.

V/O: Chris Davidson is a retired game ranger who moved here two years ago.
00:12:46
Chris: The cost of the feed is very, very high. We’ve worked it out to be about R8000 a month out of our pockets to keep these animals, to give them what they require here.

V/O: Despite this, many animals are starving to death, on average between 50 and 60 per month. They are reported on a WhatsApp group that residents also use to report sick & injured animals. The rangers are allowed to shoot animals that are suffering.

Texts: Sorted.

V/O: But they’re not what you’d call crack shots. Morné van der Walt believes his life was endangered.

Morné: I was sitting and relaxing at the lapa there. And the next moment, they were shooting the kudu. The kudu was shot right there in our property.

Mac: Almost like where this buck is?

Morné: Ja, almost there. And I mean, I’m in the line of fire or our lapa, and that's why I was so annoyed.

Mac: When you spoke to the Rangers, what did they say?

Morné: I tried to communicate with them, but there was no reaction. They loaded the carcass, and they were off!

V/O: Last year Davidson called the rangers to attend to an injured warthog.

Chris: The warthog was lying there, and our ranger walked in. So, he went to the braai here behind me and he took a dead rest out on the braai to sort of line him up nicely. A straight shot to the forehead and the bullet went off. And of course, the pig squealed and thrashed about and ran off. The Ranger didn't know what to do. What got me was that this chap had a dead rest on the braai, and the warthog was ten meters from him, and he had the telescope and he missed.

V/O: This video of a sick wildebeest being shot at close range clearly shows the ranger’s inexperience with a firearm. Instead of making the rifle safe immediately after the shot, the ranger reaches for his ears

V/O: We went looking for the rangers at their quarters. But as municipal employees they have no permission to speak to the media and were very reluctant to be filmed.

Link: This is the rangers’ accommodation but attached to their quarters is this abattoir. It’s being renovated by the Municipality, clearly gearing up to process more meat.

V/O: Processing meat here would solve the red line problem, but this abattoir is still under construction and hasn’t been licenced. So why is it already in use? On a previous visit our producer found the remains of a warthog in one of the cold rooms.

Cindy: The head being cut off ready for mount, it’s got nice teeth and we found meat in the bag.

V/O: So, we asked the Nkomazi Municipality for an interview and sent them questions about the management of Marloth Park. We arrived at the Municipal offices at the requested time, but it was a no-show.

Mac: We’re looking for Mr Ripinga.

Woman: Let me call Head Office.

V/O: The woman behind desk is not the Conservation Manager. He wasn’t in that day.

Sfx: You have reached the mailbox of….

V/O: Cyril Ripinga, wasn’t taking our calls either.

Mac: For the head of communication – after being sent questions, after a request was made, which he agreed to, at any time – still no communication?

V/O: The Municipality does not have an environmental Management Plan for Marloth Park, as required by law.

Brian: As far as I know none of the members of their staff that are responsible for conservation are qualified in conservation or qualified to a level where they would be able to lead decision making.

Mac: What sort of qualifications are we looking at here if you’re saying they’re not even qualified to do what they’re doing?

Brian: Someone in charge of an undertaking like this, and taking the day-to-day management decisions, may have an Honours degree in wildlife management or conservation ecology or similar qualification.

V/O: So, what is the solution? Inside Marloth Park is the 1500-hectare Lionspruit nature reserve. There are two lions there and no houses or humans. There’s also no interdict on shooting, which means animals can be culled there.

Brian: I would immediately build bomas along the Lionspruit fence, maybe more than one.

V/O: Animals would be lured into the boma with food, then the gate would be closed behind them.

Brian: And you have a second gate into Lionspruit; and you open the gate to Lionspruit and let them walk out into Lionspruit. It can be done.

V/O: The Municipality put out a tender for this in July: it is unclear what bids were received, or if they’ve been accepted. But conservation management is the mandate of the Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Agency.

Link: Ultimate responsibility for the wildlife in Marloth Park lies with the MTPA. The buck stops with them. So, what’s their plan to alleviate the crisis there? We did ask for an interview, and they ignored our request, saying they had to prepare for the state of the province address.

V/O: Meanwhile the state of Marloth Park remains bleak – with malnourished animals begging for food or facing starvation.

V/O: This woman wants to hide her identity for fear of being targeted. Marlene: I was sitting in my swimming pool that's close to the road. And they came driving up and they shot that kudu cow right in front of me while I'm sitting in the pool. What if - I know now the way these guys shoot because they normally shoot an animal that's hurt or anything five, six shots before they kill it. Dawie: I was sitting inside my house one evening watching television. I heard the shot, and it was right in front of my house, and I thought this is not on. V/O: Dawie Fourie has lived in Marloth Park for 27 years and belongs to the Ratepayers’ Association. Dawie: And we started enquiring like where is your licence to hunt. They couldn’t produce a licence. No competency certificate, and the gun didn’t belong to the person shooting. It belongs to the municipality. So, you actually had to have a letter from the municipality authorizing to use it. So, he had none of the documentation with him. All the houses from where he shot that animal was within less than 60 metres of where he was shooting. V/O: But Evan believes these fears were exaggerated. Mac: So, there was monitoring and supervision, they weren’t just going willy-nilly and shooting? Evan: Not a chance. I mean, we would issue them bullets. And at the end of the session, you count the carcasses, you count the bullets. You know, it's not just a haring around here and blasting away. Not at all. Cindy: It’s not good practice because of the risk factor. And they were using an abattoir that was 37km away from Marloth Park over the red line, what we call the red line because this is a foot and mouth area. V/O: The N4 is the Red Line, a veterinary fence that controls the spread of animal diseases. The Ratepayers felt so strongly that they took the Municipality to Court. In 2017 they obtained an interdict against the shooting of animals in Marloth Park. Prof: Technically the interdict put a stop to the culling of animals, but the issue was not culling animals. The issue was using high powered rifles in a residential area. V/O: Professor Brian Reilly teaches at the University of the Free State and is former Head of Department of Nature Conservation at Tshwane University of Technology. In 2018 he did a veld assessment of Marloth Park. Prof: The number of animals, the biomass of animals have exceeded the resource’s ability to carry them. So now, in that situation, the only option you have is to either remove the animals or to supplementary feed the animals. V/O: And with culling at an end, that’s what’s been happening in Marloth Park for years. This huge delivery of grass was donated by one of the homeowners. Residents collect their bales along with buckets of molasses to mix with the grass. Spar link: So, to show you how dire and serious the situation is. This is a shopping centre in Marloth Park, but it’s the only Spar in the country that sells game feed. Let’s go check. V/O: It was sold out, but the manager gave us their monthly sales volume. . Deleen: I’ve worked it out at about 1080 5kg bags a month. Mac: That’s a lot hey? Deleen: It’s a lot. V/O: In fact, that works out to 5.6 tons of pellets sold at that outlet alone. Then there’s a small business that delivers 40kg bags to residents. They move 3.2 tons of game pellets per week. They also deliver 20kg bales of lucerne – 300 of them per week. They’re supplying almost 37 tons of game feed per month. Chris: Ja, without the homeowners in Marloth, there wouldn’t be a live animal on Marloth right now. V/O: Chris Davidson is a retired game ranger who moved here two years ago. 00:12:46 Chris: The cost of the feed is very, very high. We’ve worked it out to be about R8000 a month out of our pockets to keep these animals, to give them what they require here. V/O: Despite this, many animals are starving to death, on average between 50 and 60 per month. They are reported on a WhatsApp group that residents also use to report sick & injured animals. The rangers are allowed to shoot animals that are suffering. Texts: Sorted. V/O: But they’re not what you’d call crack shots. Morné van der Walt believes his life was endangered. Morné: I was sitting and relaxing at the lapa there. And the next moment, they were shooting the kudu. The kudu was shot right there in our property. Mac: Almost like where this buck is? Morné: Ja, almost there. And I mean, I’m in the line of fire or our lapa, and that's why I was so annoyed. Mac: When you spoke to the Rangers, what did they say? Morné: I tried to communicate with them, but there was no reaction. They loaded the carcass, and they were off! V/O: Last year Davidson called the rangers to attend to an injured warthog. Chris: The warthog was lying there, and our ranger walked in. So, he went to the braai here behind me and he took a dead rest out on the braai to sort of line him up nicely. A straight shot to the forehead and the bullet went off. And of course, the pig squealed and thrashed about and ran off. The Ranger didn't know what to do. What got me was that this chap had a dead rest on the braai, and the warthog was ten meters from him, and he had the telescope and he missed. V/O: This video of a sick wildebeest being shot at close range clearly shows the ranger’s inexperience with a firearm. Instead of making the rifle safe immediately after the shot, the ranger reaches for his ears V/O: We went looking for the rangers at their quarters. But as municipal employees they have no permission to speak to the media and were very reluctant to be filmed. Link: This is the rangers’ accommodation but attached to their quarters is this abattoir. It’s being renovated by the Municipality, clearly gearing up to process more meat. V/O: Processing meat here would solve the red line problem, but this abattoir is still under construction and hasn’t been licenced. So why is it already in use? On a previous visit our producer found the remains of a warthog in one of the cold rooms. Cindy: The head being cut off ready for mount, it’s got nice teeth and we found meat in the bag. V/O: So, we asked the Nkomazi Municipality for an interview and sent them questions about the management of Marloth Park. We arrived at the Municipal offices at the requested time, but it was a no-show. Mac: We’re looking for Mr Ripinga. Woman: Let me call Head Office. V/O: The woman behind desk is not the Conservation Manager. He wasn’t in that day. Sfx: You have reached the mailbox of…. V/O: Cyril Ripinga, wasn’t taking our calls either. Mac: For the head of communication – after being sent questions, after a request was made, which he agreed to, at any time – still no communication? V/O: The Municipality does not have an environmental Management Plan for Marloth Park, as required by law. Brian: As far as I know none of the members of their staff that are responsible for conservation are qualified in conservation or qualified to a level where they would be able to lead decision making. Mac: What sort of qualifications are we looking at here if you’re saying they’re not even qualified to do what they’re doing? Brian: Someone in charge of an undertaking like this, and taking the day-to-day management decisions, may have an Honours degree in wildlife management or conservation ecology or similar qualification. V/O: So, what is the solution? Inside Marloth Park is the 1500-hectare Lionspruit nature reserve. There are two lions there and no houses or humans. There’s also no interdict on shooting, which means animals can be culled there. Brian: I would immediately build bomas along the Lionspruit fence, maybe more than one. V/O: Animals would be lured into the boma with food, then the gate would be closed behind them. Brian: And you have a second gate into Lionspruit; and you open the gate to Lionspruit and let them walk out into Lionspruit. It can be done. V/O: The Municipality put out a tender for this in July: it is unclear what bids were received, or if they’ve been accepted. But conservation management is the mandate of the Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Agency. Link: Ultimate responsibility for the wildlife in Marloth Park lies with the MTPA. The buck stops with them. So, what’s their plan to alleviate the crisis there? We did ask for an interview, and they ignored our request, saying they had to prepare for the state of the province address. V/O: Meanwhile the state of Marloth Park remains bleak – with malnourished animals begging for food or facing starvation.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Marloth Park - the bush veld holiday town shared by thousands of humans and wild animals. But there's nothing left to eat, and culling is illegal.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: It's unique in the country: an enclosed suburb, a sunset to sunrise curfew, wild animals dependent on humans for feeding, and the local municipality the only managing authority. It seemed like a good idea at the time. In 1977 Marloth Park was established as a holiday town bordering the Kruger National Park. The animals could come and go as they pleased by simply crossing the Crocodile river. But years later, when foot & mouth disease and TB became a concern, veterinary services installed a fence, effectively capturing the game inside Marloth Park. Now, 47 years and 3800 home owners later, it's over-crowded, over-grazed and the animals are dying of starvation.
metadata.Summary: Marloth Park holds 4500 residential stands each measuring 1500 m2. In between the stands are parklands which are meant for grazing. But overpopulation and mismanagement of the wildlife means there is hardly anything for the animals to eat. In 2001 the Nkomazi Local Municipality took over Marloth Park. Since then there has been no Environmental Management Plan adopted or implemented by the NKLM. Unlike other wildlife estates, there is no special levy. Residents only pay normal and fairly low municipal rates. In 2015, NKLM (who employ a Conservation manager and 12 game rangers) began a culling programme, taking off hundreds of animals to relieve the situation. But the carcasses were taken to the Mauricedale Abattoir for processing, which is across the N4, the red line which denotes a foot & mouth area. The meat was then sold with the proceeds going to the Municipality. But meat cannot be traded across the red line. In 2016 the culling programme continued, with rangers hunting animals at night, between the houses, using spotlights. However, there were reports of bullets flying through windows and into walls, thereby endangering the residents. In 2017 the Marloth Park Ratepayers Association brought an urgent interdict to stop the culling between the houses as it is illegal to shoot in a residential area without good cause, it was dangerous and put lives and properties at risk. Since then there has been a population explosion, both in animals and humans, and the Municipality seems unable to enforce basic by-laws, never mind an EMP. Neighbouring reserves like Mjejane and Sabie Sands has offered to take impala etc off their hands but the Municipality regards the animals as their assets and they want to cash in on the meat. Currently the rangers are allowed to shoot sick or injured animals, and are also picking up animals that have died from starvation. The count is between 60 and 70 animals per month. Within Marloth Park is another game reserve called Lionspruit. A solution put forward has been to capture game in temporary bomas and transport them to Lionspruit for culling.
metadata.Further information: Within Marloth Park is another game reserve called Lionspruit. A solution put forward has been to capture game in temporary bomas and transport them to Lionspruit for culling. NKLM put out a tender for this, but has not received a suitable bid. They are also building an abattoir attached to the Rangers' living quarters where they plan to process carcasses. But they already seem to be using this facility as CB found a warthog head perched on bags of meat in the cold room. Adding to the complication is an ongoing catfight between the various organisations within Marloth Park. The Ratepayers Association (560), the Property Owners Association (150), the Honorary Rangers, Marlothii Conservancy cannot agree on how the stalemate should be resolved and by whom. 1. NKLM is incompetent and not following best practice - animals are overbred, Marloth Park is over-utilised. Such mismanagement that it is becoming an ethical issue. 2. The Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Authority should have stepped in as nature conservation is a provincial competency. 3. Conflict between the residents has led to a failure of ethical wildlife management.
